teaser: A giant ape, three Gorgons and a wall of temptations stand between you and joy.
review_notes:
The image shows only the central (narrow) wall, The Hostile Forces; the lesson says so. It is a fairly low-resolution reproduction, so interactive blocks target large figures only.
Figure names (Typhoeus, Gorgons, Sickness, Madness, Death, Lasciviousness, Wantonness, Intemperance, Gnawing Grief) follow the 1902 exhibition catalog; the assignment of the three heads above the Gorgons and of the two women beside Intemperance is the usual one, please check.
Mahler conducting a wind arrangement from the Ninth Symphony at the opening: commonly reported, please confirm.
Ownership history (Carl Reininghaus 1903, Lederer family 1915, seizure 1938, purchase by the Austrian state 1973, on view in the Secession basement since 1986): please confirm dates.
Total length of about 34 m and height of about 2 m are approximate.

lesson.text: What stands between you and happiness? Most of us would answer with something vague: bad luck, other people, ourselves. In 1902 Gustav Klimt answered with a shaggy giant ape, three naked sisters with snakes in their hair, and a fat woman in a blue skirt. He painted them life-size on a wall in Vienna.

The occasion was an exhibition in honor of the composer Beethoven, held at the Secession, a building run by Vienna's rebel artists. Klimt's contribution ran along the top of three walls of a side room, about 34 meters (112 feet) in all. It retells Beethoven's Ninth Symphony as a journey: humanity longs for joy, meets its enemies, and finally reaches a choir and a kiss.

You are looking at the middle wall, the shortest of the three, and the darkest chapter. The exhibition catalog called it The Hostile Forces. A visitor in 1902 walked in and found this wall straight ahead, with the hopeful beginning on the left and the happy ending on the right. Start with the monsters.

lesson.title: The enemies outside
lesson.text: The left half of the wall belongs to a family of monsters.

spots.title: Typhoeus
spots.text: A giant from Greek myth, here an ape with a gap-toothed grin and pale, staring eyes. The catalog says even the gods fought him in vain.

spots.title: The three Gorgons
spots.text: His daughters. In myth their gaze turns people to stone. Klimt makes them slim, pale and fashionable, with gold snakes coiled in their black hair.

spots.title: Sickness, Madness, Death
spots.text: Above the Gorgons, gaunt mask-like heads peer down. The catalog names them Sickness, Madness and Death, the things no one can argue with.

lesson.text: Notice how little they do. Nobody attacks. The Gorgons pose, Typhoeus just stares, a huge brown mass of fur blocking the way. Klimt drew his monsters with long, wavy outlines and almost no shading, the flat, decorative line of Art Nouveau, the style called Jugendstil in Vienna. Evil here is elegant, which makes it more unsettling.

At the opening, the composer Gustav Mahler, then director of the Vienna opera, conducted a group of wind players in his own arrangement of a passage from the Ninth Symphony. Painting, sculpture, architecture and music were meant to merge into one experience.

Sickness and death come from outside. On the other side of the ape, Klimt placed a second group, and these enemies are the kind we invite in. The catalog lists them as Lasciviousness, Wantonness and Intemperance: lust, reckless pleasure and excess.

lesson.title: The enemies within
lesson.text: Three women to the right of the giant.

spots.title: Lasciviousness
spots.text: A woman curls up under a cloud of red hair dotted with blue flowers, her face half hidden. Klimt's red-haired women always signal desire.

spots.title: Wantonness
spots.text: Behind her, a blonde head tilts back with closed eyes and a dreamy smile. She is lost in her own pleasure and notices nobody.

spots.title: Intemperance
spots.text: A heavy woman with a great round belly, loaded with jewelry, wears a blue skirt covered in gold discs. She stands for too much of everything.

lesson.text: That blue and gold skirt is not only paint. Klimt worked on dry plaster with casein, a milk-based paint, then added gold leaf, mother-of-pearl, pieces of mirror and colored glass, even buttons and curtain rings. His father had been a gold engraver. In the room, the ornaments catch the light and the monsters glitter.

Many Viennese critics were disgusted. The naked Gorgons and the swollen body of Intemperance were called obscene and ugly, and some writers said the frieze belonged in a temple of vice, not an exhibition. The scandal helped bring a record number of visitors.

Now move right, past the women. The wall changes completely. For meters there is nothing but the giant's blue-gray wings and the coils of his snake body, patterned like peacock feathers and scales. In all that pattern, Klimt left a single human being.
One thin figure stands apart from everyone else, alone in the giant's coils. Where?

spots.title: Gnawing Grief
spots.text: An emaciated woman wrapped in a thin gray veil hunches with her head bowed and her arms pulled in. The catalog calls her Gnawing Grief. Sorrow keeps no company.

lesson.text: She is the opposite of Intemperance in every way: bony where the other is round, gray where the other is gold, alone where the others cluster. The long empty stretch around her works like a held note in music. Klimt lets the eye rest on pattern before the story picks up again on the next wall, where the arts lead humanity to joy.

None of this was meant to last. The frieze was built as a temporary decoration, to be knocked off the walls when the show closed. A collector bought it instead and had it sawn into sections. It was later seized from its Jewish owners by the Nazis, and the Austrian state bought it only in 1973. Since 1986 it has had its own room in the basement of the Secession.
Klimt gave fear and temptation a body and a pattern. On this wall the obstacles to happiness are not explained, they are dressed in gold and made impossible to walk around.

quiz.question: Which piece of music does the frieze retell?
quiz.explanation: It was made for a 1902 exhibition in honor of Beethoven and follows his Ninth Symphony.

quiz.question: Who is the giant ape at the center of the monsters?
options: Typhoeus, a giant from Greek myth
quiz.explanation: The catalog names him Typhoeus, against whom even the gods fought in vain.

quiz.question: What does the heavy woman in the blue and gold skirt stand for?
quiz.explanation: She represents too much of everything.

quiz.question: Besides paint, what did Klimt put on the wall?
options: Gold leaf, mother-of-pearl, glass, even buttons
quiz.explanation: He added real materials so that the surface would glitter.

quiz.question: What was supposed to happen to the frieze after the exhibition?
options: It would be given to Beethoven's family
quiz.explanation: It was a temporary decoration, saved because a collector bought it.

facts.text: The wall shown here is the hopeful opening chapter of the frieze.
facts.explanation: It is the middle wall, The Hostile Forces, the darkest part of the story.

facts.text: The thin, veiled figure standing alone is called Gnawing Grief.
facts.explanation: The 1902 catalog gives her that name.

facts.text: Critics in 1902 unanimously praised the frieze as tasteful.
facts.explanation: Many called its nude figures obscene and ugly.
